questions.question: What is @WebMvcTest and what does it load?
questions.title: @WebMvcTest Purpose
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot test slice annotation that loads only the web layer components—controllers, filters, @ControllerAdvice, and MockMvc infrastructure—without starting the full application context, services, or repositories.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands slice testing and can isolate the web layer for focused controller tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test, loading the entire application context and making tests slow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that you must use @MockBean for service dependencies because @WebMvcTest explicitly excludes @Service, @Repository, and @Component beans

sections.title: What @WebMvcTest Does for You
@WebMvcTest at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|@WebMvcTest|~web-layer slice|Loads @Controller / @RestController|Auto-configures MockMvc|@ControllerAdvice + filters
rose|Excluded|~not in the slice|@Service beans|@Repository beans|@Component + DataSource
emerald|Result|~fast & focused|Starts in 1-3s|Mock services with @MockBean|A failure means a controller bug

sections.title: Testing a Controller with @WebMvcTest
When to Use @WebMvcTest
sections.content:
Use **@WebMvcTest** when you want to test just the controller logic—request mapping, validation, response structure, HTTP status codes, and error handling. It's perfect for testing REST API endpoints in isolation: verifying that POST /api/users creates a user and returns 201, or that GET /api/products?category=electronics correctly passes query parameters to the service.

Use it when you're writing **contract tests**—ensuring your API behaves as documented for frontend developers or third-party integrations. Don't use it when you need to test the full flow including database queries, transaction behavior, or service business logic—that's what @SpringBootTest with Testcontainers is for.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @MockBean for service dependencies**: Freshers often write @WebMvcTest and get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException because the controller's @Autowired service isn't loaded. You must declare it as @MockBean even if you don't stub it.
- **Using @SpringBootTest for controller tests**: Loading the full context for every test makes the suite take 5-10 minutes instead of 30 seconds. @WebMvcTest is 10x faster because it loads only MVC components.
- **Not stubbing the mock service**: If you inject @MockBean but don't call when(...).thenReturn(...), Mockito returns null by default, causing NullPointerException in your controller logic.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Test slice**: @WebMvcTest loads only web layer beans—controllers, filters, MockMvc—not services or repositories
**MockMvc auto-configured**: You get @Autowired MockMvc for free to simulate HTTP requests without starting a real server
**@MockBean required**: All service dependencies must be declared as @MockBean because @Service beans are excluded from the slice
**Fast startup**: Typically 1-3 seconds vs 10-20 seconds for @SpringBootTest because it avoids database and full context initialization
**Security included**: Spring Security configuration IS loaded by default, so you may need @WithMockUser for secured endpoints
**Specify controller**: Use @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) to load only that controller, making the test even faster
**JSON validation**: Use jsonPath() to verify response body structure without deserializing to Java objects

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-WebMvcTest is a test slice annotation that loads only the web layer components you need to test controllers. It's like unit testing for your REST endpoints. When you use it, Spring Boot starts only the controller classes, MockMvc, and web infrastructure—it doesn't load services, repositories, or the database. This makes your tests really fast, usually finishing in under two seconds. Here's the key part freshers miss: because services aren't loaded, you have to provide them as at-MockBean in your test class. So if your controller has an at-Autowired OrderService, you declare at-MockBean OrderService in the test, then use Mockito's when method to stub what it returns. I'd use at-WebMvcTest whenever I'm testing just the controller logic—like verifying that a GET endpoint returns the right JSON structure, or that a POST with invalid data returns 400 Bad Request. The mistake I see freshers make is using at-SpringBootTest for everything, which loads the entire application context and makes tests slow. at-WebMvcTest is way faster because it focuses on just the web layer, and if the test fails, you immediately know it's a controller problem, not something deeper in the service or database layer.

questions.question: How do you write a basic @WebMvcTest to verify a GET endpoint returns 200 OK?
questions.title: Basic @WebMvcTest GET Request
questions.direct_answer: You inject MockMvc with @Autowired, stub the service method using @MockBean and Mockito's when(), then call mockMvc.perform(get("/api/path")).andExpect(status().isOk()) to verify the endpoint returns HTTP 200.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on ability to write a real controller test using MockMvc—this is the number one practical coding question in fresher interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the MockMvc fluent API syntax or forgetting to stub the @MockBean service, causing NullPointerException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the test structure methodically: arrange (stub the mock), act (perform the request), assert (check status and body)

sections.title: Writing Your First MockMvc Test
sections.content:
Testing a GET endpoint with **MockMvc** follows a classic test pattern: **arrange** (set up the mock data), **act** (simulate the HTTP request), and **assert** (verify the response). MockMvc is Spring's tool for simulating HTTP requests without starting a real web server—it's like having a fake browser built into your test.

You use **@Autowired MockMvc** to inject it, then call **mockMvc.perform()** to simulate a request. The fluent API reads like English: perform a GET to this path, and expect a 200 OK status. But here's the catch freshers miss: your controller calls a service method, and that service isn't loaded in @WebMvcTest. You must **@MockBean** the service and **stub its return value** using Mockito's **when().thenReturn()** syntax. Without stubbing, the service returns null, your controller crashes with NullPointerException, and the test fails with a confusing stack trace. This is the most common interview coding question for Java freshers testing Spring applications—knowing this pattern by heart shows you've written real tests, not just read documentation.

sections.title: How a GET Flows Through MockMvc
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[MockMvc.perform
GET /api/orders/1] --> B[DispatcherServlet] B --> C[OrderController] C --> D[@MockBean OrderService
stubbed result] D --> C C --> E[JSON response] E --> F[andExpect
status + jsonPath] ```

sections.title: Complete GET Endpoint Test
When to Write This Test
sections.content:
Write a MockMvc GET test whenever you need to verify that your REST endpoint **returns the correct HTTP status** and **JSON structure**.

Use it to test happy path scenarios: GET /api/users returns a list of users with 200 OK, or GET /api/orders/123 returns a single order. It's also critical for **error cases**: test that GET /api/products/999 returns 404 Not Found when the product doesn't exist. These tests are your **API contract**—they guarantee that frontend developers or mobile apps can rely on your endpoint's behavior. They're also fast enough to run on every git push, so you catch breaking changes immediately. Don't use this for testing business logic inside the service—that belongs in service unit tests with plain JUnit and Mockito, no Spring context needed.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to stub the service**: The number one mistake is injecting at-MockBean ProductService but not calling when(productService.getAllProducts()).thenReturn(...). Mockito returns null by default, so your controller gets null from the service, tries to process it, and throws NullPointerException. The test fails with a 500 Internal Server Error instead of 200 OK.
- **Not importing static methods**: Freshers copy-paste code but forget static imports. You need import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get and import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status, or you get compilation errors.
- **Wrong jsonPath syntax**: Writing jsonPath("name") instead of jsonPath("$.name")—the dollar sign is required to reference the JSON root.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Arrange-Act-Assert pattern**: First stub the mock service (arrange), then perform the HTTP request (act), finally verify status and JSON (assert)
**MockMvc injection**: Use @Autowired MockMvc—it's auto-configured by @WebMvcTest, no manual setup needed
**Mockito stubbing required**: Call when(service.method()).thenReturn(data) before the request or the controller gets null
**Fluent API**: mockMvc.perform(get(path)).andExpect(matcher) reads like English and chains multiple assertions
**jsonPath validation**: Use jsonPath to check JSON response fields without deserializing—jsonPath("$.id").value(1) verifies the id field
**Static imports**: Import get() from MockMvcRequestBuilders and status() from MockMvcResultMatchers for clean syntax
**Exception handling**: mockMvc.perform() throws Exception, so test methods must declare throws Exception or wrap in try-catch

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test a GET endpoint, I'd start by annotating the test class with at-WebMvcTest and specifying the controller I'm testing. Then I'd inject MockMvc using at-Autowired—that's the tool Spring gives you to simulate HTTP requests. Next, I'd declare the controller's service dependency as at-MockBean because services aren't loaded in WebMvcTest. Here's the critical step freshers forget: before calling the endpoint, I have to stub the service method using Mockito. So I'd write something like when productService dot getAllProducts returns a list of test products. Then I call mockMvc dot perform with get of the API path, and chain andExpect to verify the response. For a 200 OK, I'd write andExpect status dot isOk. If I want to check the JSON body, I'd use jsonPath—like jsonPath dollar-sign bracket-zero bracket dot name dot value Laptop to verify the first product's name. The pattern is arrange, act, assert: stub the mock, perform the request, check the result. The mistake I'd avoid is forgetting to stub the service, because then it returns null and the controller throws NullPointerException, making the test fail with 500 instead of 200.

questions.question: What does @WebMvcTest NOT load and what do you have to provide yourself?
questions.title: What @WebMvcTest Excludes
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest does not load @Service, @Repository, @Component, or configuration classes marked with @Configuration. You must provide these dependencies as @MockBean in your test class, or the controller will fail with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what the slice actually excludes and how to handle missing dependencies in controller tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting NoSuchBeanDefinitionException when running the test and not knowing to add @MockBean for the missing service
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Security configuration IS loaded by default in @WebMvcTest, so you may need @WithMockUser or to exclude security auto-configuration

sections.title: What Gets Left Behind in @WebMvcTest
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest is a **surgical slice**—it loads exactly what you need for web layer testing and excludes everything else to keep tests fast. It does **not** load any beans annotated with **@Service**, **@Repository**, **@Component**, or **@Configuration**.

That means no business logic layer, no database access, no JPA repositories, no custom beans you defined in configuration classes. The **JPA EntityManager**, **DataSource**, and Hibernate aren't started. **@Scheduled** methods won't run. **@EventListener** beans won't be created. Spring Boot applies this exclusion deliberately: if your test needs the service layer, you're not testing just the controller anymore—you're testing integration, which belongs in @SpringBootTest. The consequence: when your controller has **@Autowired OrderService**, Spring can't find that bean during test context startup and throws **NoSuchBeanDefinitionException**. The solution is simple but freshers always forget it: declare the service as **@MockBean** in your test class, providing a fake implementation that you control with Mockito stubs.

sections.title: Loaded vs Excluded
sections.content:
emerald|Loaded|~web layer|@Controller / @RestController|MockMvc + Jackson|@ControllerAdvice + filters
rose|Excluded|~other layers|@Service|@Repository|@Component + DataSource
amber|You supply|~fill the gaps|@MockBean for each service|@Import for needed config

sections.title: Handling Missing Dependencies with @MockBean
When This Knowledge Matters
sections.content: This matters **every single time** you write a @WebMvcTest—you'll encounter NoSuchBeanDefinitionException on your first run if you have any @Autowired dependencies in your controller. Understanding what's excluded helps you decide: should I mock this with @MockBean, or do I actually need @SpringBootTest? Use **@MockBean** when the dependency is a service layer interface whose behavior you can stub in one line—like when(orderService.findById(1L)).thenReturn(order). Switch to **@SpringBootTest** when you need real database queries, transaction rollback, or complex service orchestration that's too painful to mock. This also matters when you get weird security errors: Spring Security **is** loaded by @WebMvcTest, so secured endpoints need **@WithMockUser** or you'll get 401 Unauthorized even with correct controller logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not reading the NoSuchBeanDefinitionException message**: Freshers panic when they see this exception and don't read the error—it explicitly tells you which bean is missing and suggests adding @MockBean. The fix takes 10 seconds if you read the message.
- **Mocking too many layers**: If you find yourself declaring five or six at-MockBean dependencies, your controller is doing too much or you should be using at-SpringBootTest. A controller should depend on 1-3 services max.
- **Forgetting Spring Security is loaded**: Freshers add at-WebMvcTest, test a secured endpoint, and get 401 Unauthorized. They assume security isn't loaded and waste time debugging. The fix: add at-WithMockUser or exclude security with at-WebMvcTest excludeAutoConfiguration equals SecurityAutoConfiguration dot class.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Excluded annotations**: @Service, @Repository, @Component, and @Configuration beans are not loaded in the test context
**No database layer**: JPA repositories, DataSource, EntityManager, and Hibernate are not initialized—no real database access
**@MockBean required**: Every @Autowired service in your controller must be declared as @MockBean in the test or you get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
**Security IS loaded**: Spring Security auto-configuration runs by default, so @PreAuthorize and @Secured annotations are enforced
**Fast by design**: Excluding these layers makes tests start in 1-3 seconds instead of 10-20 seconds for full context
**Focus on web layer**: The exclusions enforce testing only controller logic—request mapping, validation, response serialization
**@Import escape hatch**: If you really need a specific @Configuration class, you can load it with @Import(MyConfig.class) on the test class

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: at-WebMvcTest doesn't load any beans annotated with at-Service, at-Repository, or at-Component. It also skips configuration classes and the entire database layer—so no JPA repositories, no DataSource, no Hibernate. The idea is to test only the web layer in isolation, which keeps tests fast. The consequence is that if your controller has an at-Autowired dependency on OrderService, Spring can't find that bean when the test starts, and you'll get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. The fix is to declare it as at-MockBean in your test class. That tells Spring to create a mock version of the service that you control with Mockito stubs. One thing that surprises freshers: Spring Security configuration IS loaded by default. So if you're testing a secured endpoint, you need to add at-WithMockUser to simulate an authenticated user, or you'll get 401 Unauthorized even if your controller logic is correct. The pattern I follow is: look at every at-Autowired field in the controller, and declare each one as at-MockBean in the test. If you end up mocking five or six dependencies, that's a sign your controller is too fat or you should switch to at-SpringBootTest for integration testing.

questions.question: How do you test a POST endpoint with a request body using @WebMvcTest and MockMvc?
questions.title: Testing POST Endpoint with MockMvc
questions.direct_answer: Use mockMvc.perform(post("/api/path").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(jsonString)).andExpect(status().isCreated()) to test a POST endpoint. You must set the content type and provide the request body as a JSON string.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical MockMvc knowledge for POST requests—slightly harder than GET and very commonly asked in interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to set contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), which causes HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type, or not knowing how to serialize the request body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both manual JSON string construction and using ObjectMapper to serialize a Java object, and explain why content type is required

sections.title: Testing POST Endpoints with MockMvc
sections.content:
Testing a POST endpoint is slightly more complex than GET because you're **sending data to the server**, not just retrieving it. You need three things: the **HTTP method** (POST), the **content type** (telling Spring the body is JSON), and the **request body** (the actual JSON data).

MockMvc's fluent API makes this readable: perform a POST to this path, with content type APPLICATION_JSON, with this JSON content, and expect a 201 Created status. The tricky part freshers miss: **contentType()** is mandatory for POST/PUT requests with a body. If you omit it, Spring doesn't know the body is JSON, assumes it's plain text or form data, and returns **HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type**. You also need to **serialize your Java object to JSON** using either manual string concatenation (fragile but quick for demos) or **ObjectMapper** (production approach). Then you **stub the service method** that creates the resource, making it return the saved entity with an ID. Finally, you verify the response: 201 status, location header, and JSON body structure. This is the second most common Spring testing question in fresher interviews after basic GET tests—mastering it shows you can test real CRUD APIs.

sections.title: POST Request Test Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[perform POST /api/orders
JSON body] --> B[Controller
@RequestBody + @Valid] B --> C[@MockBean service
when..thenReturn] C --> D[201 Created] D --> E[andExpect status isCreated
+ jsonPath id] ```

sections.title: POST Request Test with ObjectMapper
When to Write This Test
sections.content:
Write a POST test whenever your API **creates a resource**: POST /api/users creates a user, POST /api/orders creates an order. Test that the endpoint returns **201 Created**, includes the generated ID in the response body, and optionally includes a **Location header** pointing to the new resource.

Use it to verify **request validation**: test that POST with missing required fields returns 400 Bad Request with validation error messages. Test **business rule violations**: POST /api/orders with quantity=-5 should return 400 with a meaningful error. POST tests are also critical for **contract testing**: they document what JSON structure your API expects, which frontend developers and integration partners rely on. Don't use POST tests for testing the service's internal save logic—that belongs in service unit tests with Mockito, no Spring context.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting contentType**: The number one mistake is calling perform(post(path).content(json)) without .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON). The test fails with HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type because Spring's message converters don't know the body is JSON.
- **Manual JSON with typos**: Freshers write content("{\"name\":\"Alice\"}") and forget to escape quotes or miss a comma, causing Jackson parse errors. Use ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString instead—it's safer and you can reuse the same object in multiple tests.
- **Not stubbing the service method**: Writing when(orderService.createOrder(newOrder)).thenReturn(savedOrder) expecting exact object match, but MockMvc deserializes the JSON into a different object instance. Use any(Order.class) or ArgumentMatchers.any() to match any Order argument.
- **Wrong HTTP status**: Checking status().isOk() (200) instead of status().isCreated() (201) for resource creation—REST conventions say POST should return 201, not 200.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Three required parts**: POST method via post(path), content type via contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), and JSON body via content(jsonString)
**ObjectMapper for serialization**: Inject @Autowired ObjectMapper and call writeValueAsString(object) to convert Java object to JSON safely
**Content type is mandatory**: Omitting contentType() causes 415 Unsupported Media Type because Spring can't deserialize the body
**Stub with any()**: Use when(service.createOrder(any(Order.class))) because MockMvc deserializes JSON into a new object instance
**201 Created for POST**: Resource creation should return status().isCreated(), not status().isOk()—follow REST conventions
**Verify response body**: Use jsonPath to check the generated ID and confirm the returned object matches what you posted
**Location header**: In real APIs, POST /api/orders should return Location: /api/orders/42 header—test with andExpect(header().string("Location", "/api/orders/42"))

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test a POST endpoint, I'd use mockMvc.perform with the post method, passing the API path. The key difference from GET is that POST sends data, so I need to set two things: the content type and the request body. I'd call .contentType with MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON to tell Spring the body is JSON, then .content with the actual JSON string. For the JSON, I have two options. I can write it manually like content of open-brace quote-name-quote colon quote-Alice-quote close-brace, but that's error-prone with escaped quotes. The better way is to inject ObjectMapper and call writeValueAsString on my Java object—Spring automatically serializes it to JSON. Before performing the request, I'd stub the service method with Mockito, something like when orderService.createOrder with any Order.class returns a saved order with an ID. Then I'd chain andExpect to verify the response. For POST, I'd expect status dot isCreated—that's HTTP 201—not 200 OK. I'd also use jsonPath to verify the generated ID is in the response body. The mistake freshers make is forgetting to set the content type, which causes HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type. Another mistake is stubbing with the exact object instead of any, so the stub doesn't match because MockMvc deserializes JSON into a different instance. This pattern works for any resource creation endpoint—users, orders, products—just change the path and object type.

questions.question: How do you test that a controller returns a 404 when a resource is not found?
questions.title: Testing 404 in @WebMvcTest
questions.direct_answer: Stub the @MockBean service to throw a custom ResourceNotFoundException using when().thenThrow(), then assert .andExpect(status().isNotFound()) in the MockMvc call. You also need a @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler to map the exception to HTTP 404.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to test error paths and exception handling in Spring controllers—not just the happy path where everything succeeds
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing tests that only verify successful cases and forgetting to test edge cases like missing resources, which are critical for production-ready APIs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that without @ControllerAdvice or @ExceptionHandler, the exception becomes a 500 Internal Server Error—showing you understand Spring's exception handling chain

sections.title: Testing 404 Responses in Spring Controllers
sections.content:
Testing 404 responses verifies that your API handles missing resources gracefully instead of crashing or returning misleading errors. When a service throws a **ResourceNotFoundException**, Spring doesn't automatically convert it to HTTP 404—you need explicit wiring. The test has three parts: (1) stub the mock service to throw the exception, (2) perform the HTTP request with MockMvc, and (3) assert the response status is 404.

Think of it like a theater rehearsal: the service (actor) throws its line (exception), the @ControllerAdvice (director) interprets it, and MockMvc (audience) verifies the performance. Without the director, the actor's improvisation becomes a 500 error—a generic "something went wrong" instead of the precise "resource not found" message clients expect. This pattern is crucial because production APIs must distinguish between "you asked for something that doesn't exist" (client error, 404) and "our system failed" (server error, 500).

sections.title: How a 404 Is Produced and Asserted
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[GET /api/orders/99] --> B[Controller] B --> C[service returns
Optional.empty] C --> D[throw NotFound

sections.title: Testing 404 with MockMvc and Exception Handling
When to Test 404 Responses
sections.content: Use this pattern when testing REST APIs that fetch resources by ID, username, or any unique identifier—endpoints like GET /api/users/{id} or GET /api/products/{sku}. Test 404s for search endpoints that might return empty results, like GET /api/orders?status=SHIPPED when no shipped orders exist. Also test 404s in delete operations: DELETE /api/comments/{id} should return 404 if the comment was already deleted or never existed, not 200 OK. In real applications, clients rely on 404 to implement retry logic, caching strategies, and user feedback—"Product not found" is better UX than "Something went wrong."

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ControllerAdvice**: Writing the test without the exception handler, then wondering why it returns 500 instead of 404—Spring doesn't magically know your exception means "not found." **Testing only the happy path**: Writing five tests for successful orders but zero tests for missing orders, leaving production code vulnerable to NPEs or generic 500 errors when resources don't exist.
- **Throwing generic RuntimeException**: Using throw new RuntimeException("not found") instead of a semantic exception like ResourceNotFoundException, making it impossible to distinguish "resource missing" from "database connection failed" in exception handlers.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **when().thenThrow()**: Mockito method that stubs a service call to throw an exception instead of returning a value—essential for testing error paths
**@ControllerAdvice**: Spring annotation for global exception handlers that apply to all controllers—without it, exceptions become 500 errors
**@ExceptionHandler**: Method-level annotation that maps specific exception types to HTTP responses—like catch blocks for controllers
**@ResponseStatus**: Annotation that sets the HTTP status code for an exception handler—NOT_FOUND maps to 404
**status().isNotFound()**: MockMvc assertion that verifies HTTP 404 response—equivalent to checking status code 404
**ResourceNotFoundException**: Custom exception class for missing resources—better than generic RuntimeException because handlers can target it specifically
**jsonPath assertion**: Verifies the error message in the response body—not just the status code—so clients get useful feedback

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test that a controller returns 404 when a resource isn't found, you need three pieces working together. First, stub your mock service to throw a ResourceNotFoundException using when orderService.findById then-throw. This simulates the database not finding the record. Second, use MockMvc to perform the GET request and assert status is-not-found—that's the 404 check. But here's the critical part freshers often miss: you also need a controller-advice class with an exception-handler method. Without that, Spring doesn't know your custom exception means "not found"—it'll just return 500 internal server error. The exception handler catches ResourceNotFoundException and uses response-status NOT_FOUND to map it to HTTP 404. You can also assert the response body using jsonPath to verify the error message is helpful, like "Order not found" instead of a generic stack trace. In real APIs, this distinction matters because clients use 404 to trigger different logic than 500—maybe retry on 500 but show a "product unavailable" page on 404. The pattern is: mock throws exception, controller-advice catches it, handler maps to 404, MockMvc verifies the whole chain. That's how you test error paths properly, not just happy paths where everything exists.

questions.question: What is the difference between @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest for testing a controller?
questions.title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest for Controllers
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer—controllers, filters, and MockMvc—and starts in 2-5 seconds. @SpringBootTest loads the full application context including services, repositories, and database connections, taking 10-20 seconds, but it tests the complete application wiring end-to-end.

interviewer_intent.testing: Decision-making ability—knowing when to use fast, focused unit tests versus slower, comprehensive integration tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every controller test, making the test suite take minutes to run and hiding the real source of failures behind layers of autowiring
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete decision rule: use @WebMvcTest to verify controller logic and HTTP contracts in isolation, @SpringBootTest to verify the full stack works together with real database and service interactions

sections.title: Choosing Between @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest is a **slice test** annotation that loads only the components needed to test Spring MVC controllers—the web layer. It starts MockMvc, scans for @Controller and @RestController classes, and configures the HTTP request/response infrastructure, but skips services, repositories, and database connections. @SpringBootTest is a **full-context test** that loads your entire Spring Boot application exactly as it runs in production—every @Service, @Repository, @Configuration, and even external connections like databases or message queues.

The key trade-off is speed versus completeness. @WebMvcTest is fast because it loads 5-10 beans instead of 50-100, but you must mock all dependencies with @MockBean. @SpringBootTest is slow because it initializes everything, but it catches wiring mistakes and integration issues that slice tests miss. Think of @WebMvcTest as testing a single stage of a pipeline in isolation, while @SpringBootTest tests the entire factory floor running together.

sections.title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest
sections.content:
blue|@WebMvcTest|~slice test|Web layer only|MockMvc auto-configured|1-3s startup
violet|@SpringBootTest|~full context|All beans + real DB|TestRestTemplate / full server|10-20s startup
emerald|Rule of thumb|~pick one|Controller logic -> @WebMvcTest|Full flow + DB -> @SpringBootTest

rows: Full integration including DB and services

sections.title: Same Controller, Two Test Styles
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@WebMvcTest** when you're testing controller behavior in isolation: validating request mappings, checking HTTP status codes, verifying JSON serialization, or testing @Valid input validation. For example, testing that POST /api/orders with invalid data returns 400 Bad Request with field errors.

Use **@SpringBootTest** when you need to verify the full stack works together: testing that an order creation endpoint actually saves to the database, triggers email notifications, and updates inventory counts. Also use it for testing security configurations, database transactions spanning multiple services, or any scenario where mocking would hide real integration issues. A good rule: if the test name includes "integration" or "end-to-end," use @SpringBootTest. If it includes "controller" or "endpoint," use @WebMvcTest.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for everything**: Running every controller test with full context startup, making your test suite take 10 minutes to run when it could take 2 minutes—developers stop running tests before commits.
- **Not mocking in @WebMvcTest**: Forgetting to add @MockBean for services, then getting confused by NoSuchBeanDefinitionException errors—@WebMvcTest doesn't load services automatically.
- **Testing business logic in @WebMvcTest**: Verifying complex service behavior in a controller test instead of unit testing the service separately—controller tests should verify HTTP concerns, not business rules.
- **Mixing concerns**: Using @SpringBootTest but still mocking everything with @MockBean, defeating the purpose of loading the full context—at that point, use @WebMvcTest.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@WebMvcTest**: Slice test annotation that loads only the web layer—controllers, MockMvc, and HTTP infrastructure—but not services or repositories
**@SpringBootTest**: Full-context test annotation that loads the entire application as it runs in production—all beans and external connections
**MockMvc**: Provided automatically by @WebMvcTest for making HTTP requests in tests—not available by default in @SpringBootTest unless you add @AutoConfigureMockMvc
**@MockBean**: Required in @WebMvcTest to provide stub implementations of services and repositories—Spring won't autowire real beans
**Startup time**: @WebMvcTest is 4-8x faster because it loads fewer beans—critical for keeping test feedback loops short
**Test pyramid**: Most tests should use @WebMvcTest (unit/slice tests at the base), fewer should use @SpringBootTest (integration tests at the top)
**@AutoConfigureMockMvc**: Annotation to add MockMvc support to @SpringBootTest—needed if you want both full context and MockMvc together

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference is what gets loaded and how fast the test starts. Web-mvc-test loads only the web layer—your controllers, filters, and MockMvc—so it starts in about two to five seconds. Spring-boot-test loads your entire application context including services, repositories, database connections, everything, so it takes ten to twenty seconds or more. The speed difference matters when you're running hundreds of tests. Web-mvc-test is a slice test, meaning it focuses on one slice of your application—the HTTP layer. You have to use mock-bean to stub any services your controller depends on because they're not loaded. Spring-boot-test is a full integration test. All your beans are autowired for real, and you can test that the whole stack works together—like verifying an order actually gets saved to the database. Here's the decision rule I follow: use web-mvc-test when testing controller logic in isolation—things like request validation, status codes, and JSON responses. Use spring-boot-test when you need to verify end-to-end behavior—like checking that creating an order updates inventory and sends an email. A common mistake is using spring-boot-test for every test because it seems easier—you don't have to think about mocking. But that makes your test suite painfully slow, and when tests fail, it's harder to know if the controller broke or the database connection broke. Web-mvc-test gives you fast feedback on controller issues specifically.

questions.question: How do you use jsonPath() in MockMvc to assert on the response body?
questions.title: Using jsonPath() in MockMvc
questions.direct_answer: jsonPath() is a MockMvc assertion method that uses JsonPath expressions to navigate and assert on JSON response bodies. You write jsonPath dollar-dot-field-name dot-value expected-value to verify that a field in the JSON response matches what you expect—the dollar sign represents the root object of the JSON response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of MockMvc response verification—jsonPath is the standard way to assert on JSON responses in Spring controller tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only checking HTTP status codes without verifying response content, or not understanding JsonPath syntax like dollar-dot for fields and dollar-bracket-zero for array elements
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both simple field assertions and complex nested or array assertions, and explain that jsonPath is better than manually deserializing JSON because it's more readable and handles missing fields gracefully

sections.title: Using jsonPath() to Assert on JSON Responses
sections.content:
**jsonPath()** is a MockMvc matcher that lets you navigate into JSON response bodies and assert on specific fields using **JsonPath expressions**—a query language for JSON similar to XPath for XML. Instead of deserializing the entire response into a Java object, you write expressions like **$.userId** to access the userId field at the root level, or **$.address.city** to navigate nested objects, or **$[0].name** to access the first element in an array. The dollar sign represents the JSON root, dot notation navigates into objects, and bracket notation accesses array elements.

Think of it like CSS selectors for JSON: just as you write div.container to target HTML elements, you write $.order.items[0] to target JSON fields. This approach is better than manual deserialization because (1) it's more readable—the assertion reads like the JSON structure, (2) it handles missing fields gracefully with clear error messages, and (3) it's faster to write—no need for mapping classes. JsonPath is the industry standard for JSON assertions in Spring tests, used in millions of test suites.

sections.title: jsonPath Assertions for Different JSON Structures
When to Use jsonPath Assertions
sections.content:
Use **jsonPath()** whenever you need to verify that a REST endpoint returns the correct JSON structure and values—basically every controller test that checks response bodies.

Use it to assert on specific fields after creating or updating resources: POST /api/products should return the new product ID, and you'd verify jsonPath dollar-dot-id exists.

Use it to test pagination metadata: GET /api/users?page=2 should return jsonPath dollar-dot-totalPages.

Use it to verify error responses have the right structure: a 400 response should have jsonPath dollar-dot-errors-bracket-zero-dot-field containing the field name that failed validation. In real applications, clients depend on the exact JSON structure—mobile apps parse responses into UI components, so testing the JSON contract prevents breaking changes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only checking status codes**: Writing tests that verify status is-ok but never check the response body—like testing a vending machine gives you something but not checking if it's the right snack.
- **Wrong JsonPath syntax**: Writing jsonPath dollar-bracket-field-bracket instead of jsonPath dollar-dot-field, or forgetting the dollar sign entirely—JsonPath is picky about syntax.
- **Not testing null or missing fields**: Only testing the happy path where all fields are present, then production code breaks when optional fields are missing—use exists() or doesNotExist() matchers.
- **Deserializing manually**: Writing code to parse the JSON response into a Java object with ObjectMapper just to assert one field—overkill when jsonPath can do it in one line.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **jsonPath()**: MockMvc matcher for asserting on JSON response bodies using JsonPath query expressions—the standard way to verify JSON in Spring tests
**$ (dollar sign)**: Represents the root of the JSON document in JsonPath expressions—all paths start with this symbol
**Dot notation**: $.field.nested accesses nested object properties—like navigating folders in a file system
**Bracket notation**: $[0] accesses array elements by index, starting from zero—similar to Java array access
**value() matcher**: Asserts that a JsonPath expression evaluates to a specific value—can compare strings, numbers, or booleans
**exists() and doesNotExist()**: Matchers to verify whether a field is present in the JSON—useful for optional fields
**isArray()**: Matcher to verify that a JsonPath expression points to a JSON array—catches type mismatches early

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: json-path is a method you use with MockMvc to assert on the JSON response body. You give it a JsonPath expression—basically a query string—that navigates into the JSON structure, and then you check if the value matches what you expect. For example, json-path dollar-dot-name dot-value Alice checks that the name field at the root level equals Alice. The dollar sign means the root of the JSON response, and the dot navigates into fields. If you have nested objects, you chain dots—like dollar-dot-address-dot-city to get the city inside the address object. For arrays, you use bracket notation with an index. json-path dollar-bracket-zero-dot-id gets the id field of the first element in the array. You can also use length to check array size, or exists to verify a field is present even if you don't care about its value. The reason json-path is better than deserializing the JSON manually is it's way more readable and explicit. When I see json-path dollar-dot-order-dot-total in a test, I immediately know we're checking the total field inside the order object. If I deserialize into a Java class, I have to trace through object mapping code. Also, json-path gives helpful error messages when a field is missing—manual deserialization might throw null-pointer-exception. Every Spring controller test that verifies response content uses json-path. It's the standard approach because it's concise, type-safe enough for tests, and works with complex nested structures without writing mapping classes.
